illustration.alt: Partners carrying briefcases leave Weil’s New York office while employees watch Barry Wolf address them on a monitor and rows of costly desks remain behind.

elementaryChecklist.financialMechanism: A partner run: rainmaking partners take client revenue elsewhere while rent, staff, and other fixed costs remain, reducing profits and prompting still more partners to leave.
elementaryChecklist.centralJoke: A profitable law firm can collapse because its partners foresee that others may leave—and lawyer-friendly rules protecting their freedom to leave help everyone rush out at once.

preschool.title: The Run on Weil
preschool.lesson: When client-bringing partners leave a law firm but its fixed costs remain, expected profits fall and encourage more partners to leave, creating a self-fulfilling run.
paragraphs:
At Weil Gotshal & Manges, by Central Park’s southeast side,
a nearly century-old law firm worked with corporate pride.
It brought in nearly $2.1 billion just last year,
yet prominent partners started leaving—and the future looked less clear.

Bloomberg’s Roy Strom reported the firm would soon wind down;
employees heard Barry Wolf on Zoom, with somber looks around.
Wolf was set to yield control; merger talks had failed as well—
the talks with Willkie Farr & Gallagher could not rescue Weil.

Yale’s John Morley explained how partner runs can grow:
a “rainmaker” brings clients—and their fees may also go.
But office rent and staff costs do not vanish through the door;
with less profit left to share, the next star may want more.

A rival offers better pay; another takes the flight,
which makes departure seem still wiser to the partners left that night.
The firm may still be profitable—that’s the strange surprise:
partners see what could come later, so they hurry toward the exits.

And lawyers’ ethics rules generally bar noncompetes that block the way;
the freedom each lawyer prizes lets the whole firm drain away.
A rule that helps each lawyer leave for somewhere good and new
can help unravel the profitable firm they’re leaving, too.

What happened? After prominent partner exits and failed merger talks with Willkie Farr & Gallagher, Weil Gotshal & Manges said it would wind down despite earning nearly $2.1 billion in revenue the prior year. Because client-bringing partners can leave quickly while fixed costs remain, each exit lowers expected profits and encourages more departures, creating a self-fulfilling run.

illustration.alt: William Evarts carries a law degree and corporate refinancing plans from PJT Partners toward Sidley Austin, where lawyers await him beside a liability management table as a Chapter 11 courthouse is bypassed.

elementaryChecklist.financialMechanism: Liability management lawyers design refinancing transactions that reshape corporate debts outside court, helping companies avoid formal Chapter 11 bankruptcy reorganizations.
elementaryChecklist.centralJoke: Lawyers traditionally left for investment banking because it paid better; now a banker is moving to a law firm because elite law can pay better, and legal practice experience is nearly optional while law credentials remain mandatory.

preschool.title: The Banker Who Went to a Law Firm
preschool.lesson: Sidley Austin hired investment banker William Evarts to lead liability management work: refinancing troubled companies’ debts outside court to help them avoid Chapter 11, while legal ethics made his law credentials important even though he had never practiced law.
paragraphs:
Sujeet Indap reported a curious career turn:
A banker joined lawyers—with much still to learn.
William Evarts, at PJT since 2015,
Advised companies when their debt plans turned mean.

Now Sidley Austin has hired him away
To lead “liability management” day after day.
That group reshapes loans and refinances debt,
So Chapter 11 might be avoided yet.

Evarts has an MBA and a law degree too,
Though practicing law was a thing he did not do.
That path to a top law-firm post is quite rare—
But winning new clients is prized everywhere.

A leader brings business and trusted advice;
Restructuring banking can train both skills nicely.
Yet ethics rules say lawyers must run the firm,
So Evarts’s law degree helped satisfy that term.

Once lawyers chose banking because banking paid more;
Now bankers eye law firms—and walk through their door.
Top lawyers can earn over $20 million a year:
The career ladder flipped, with the punch line quite clear.

What happened? Sidley Austin hired PJT Partners banker William Evarts to lead a legal team that designs out-of-court debt refinancings for companies trying to avoid Chapter 11. His move was unusual because he had never practiced law, though he holds a law degree, and booming top-lawyer pay helped reverse the traditional flow from law into banking.

illustration.alt: Adam Ash and University of Chicago students hand out onions while rallying outside the Chicago Mercantile Exchange as puzzled passersby watch.

elementaryChecklist.financialMechanism: Futures contracts lock in a price now for a commodity delivered later. U.S. law has prohibited futures trading in onions for 68 years, and the students argued that modern market-manipulation rules made the special ban outdated.
elementaryChecklist.centralJoke: A group of students held an utterly deadpan, apparently sincere protest for the freedom to trade onion futures, making observers wonder whether it was performance art, a PR stunt, or a joke about The Onion; Kalshi’s later involvement made it not quite sponsored content, but sort of.

preschool.title: The Very Serious Onion March
preschool.lesson: Onion futures—contracts setting a price now for onions delivered later—have been banned in the United States for 68 years; For Our Futures wants the ban repealed, and Kalshi became involved after the rally was already planned.
paragraphs:
Outside the Chicago Mercantile Exchange one day,
University of Chicago students gave onions away.

For Our Futures marched, with Adam Ash at the fore:
“Let onion-futures trading be banned no more!”

A future lets traders agree now to pay
a set price for onions delivered someday.

That trade has been banned in the U.S. for sixty-eight years,
so the students brought onions and perfectly serious cheers.

Was this performance art? Was it PR on display?
Was it a joke for The Onion? They solemnly said, “No way.”

Adam said it wasn’t America’s biggest law at all;
that was why changing it could be a practical call.

Stronger rules against market tricks now exist, they explained,
so why should this odd prohibition remain?

Bloomberg’s Erin Ailworth reported the scene,
and finance experts debated what trading should mean.

Kalshi’s Tarek Mansour called the students “patriots” online;
a company that favors more tradable events liked their design.

But Kalshi joined only after the rally was planned and declared,
so it wasn’t strictly sponsored content—just kind of, once shared.

What happened? For Our Futures rallied to repeal the 68-year-old U.S. ban on onion futures, which are contracts to trade onions later at a price agreed upon now. Kalshi became involved only after the students had planned and announced the event.

illustration.alt: Kalshi co-founders Tarek Mansour and Luana Lopes Lara stand between Derek Brown’s Utah criminal complaint and a contradictory CFTC order to keep sports-event contracts available nationwide.

elementaryChecklist.financialMechanism: Kalshi offers event contracts whose payouts depend on sports outcomes; Utah treats those trades as illegal gambling, while the CFTC regulates Kalshi federally and ordered it to continue offering markets nationwide.
elementaryChecklist.centralJoke: Kalshi was caught between opposite legal commands: Utah said it was illegal to offer sports bets there, while its federal regulator’s orders made it illegal for Kalshi not to offer them.

preschool.title: The Bets That Must—and Mustn’t—Be Offered
preschool.lesson: Utah’s gambling law and a federal court ruling told Kalshi to stop offering sports bets in Utah, while its federal regulator, the CFTC, ordered Kalshi to keep its markets available nationwide.
paragraphs:
For 130 years, Utah’s rule has been clear:
“No sports-gambling bets may be offered in here.”
But Kalshi let customers trade contracts on games,
with payouts decided by outcomes and names.

Kalshi asked federal court: “Can Utah’s law apply?”
The judge answered yes, rejecting its reply.
Still Utahns could trade on sports events online.
Utah officials said, “That crosses the line.”

On Wednesday, Utah filed criminal charges and named
Kalshi Inc., Tarek Mansour, and Luana Lopes Lara as defendants in the complaint.
Attorney General Derek Brown said the court had been clear:
“Kalshi kept taking bets. We’re stopping it here.”

Kalshi called it “crazy overreach” and politics in play,
and said it would fight the charges in court right away.
But Kalshi’s federal regulator—the CFTC—
had issued a very different decree.

Using “statutory emergency powers,” it ordered nationwide trade,
and sued to overturn Utah’s ban as it stayed.
So offering bets was illegal, Utah declared;
not offering bets broke federal orders Kalshi was required to obey.

Kalshi helped tie this remarkable snare,
with two opposite commands both waiting there.
Perhaps the Supreme Court will someday decide
which government’s order the market must abide.

What happened? Utah charged Kalshi and its co-founders after Kalshi continued offering sports bets despite a federal ruling that Utah’s gambling laws applied. At the same time, the CFTC ordered federally regulated Kalshi to keep offering its markets nationwide, creating directly conflicting commands.
